chunks.title: Viral conjunctivitis (EKC)
chunks.tldr: Follicles on lower lid + tender preauricular node, watery, one eye then the other, after a cold. Adenovirus 8, 19, 37 (EKC); 3, 7 = pharyngoconjunctival fever (kids). Worse days 4–7, lasts 2–3 weeks, contagious ~10–12 days. Rx: hygiene, cool compresses, PF tears; peel membranes; steroids for membranes or vision-reducing SEIs (1–2 weeks later). No routine antibiotics.
points: Early sign: intraepithelial microcysts.
Acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis: enterovirus 70, coxsackie A24 (tropics).
Steroids shorten symptoms but prolong shedding; SEIs can rebound on taper; only after slit-lamp exam.
Antihistamine drop for itch.
Off work/school while red and weeping.
HSV conjunctivitis: unilateral follicular + lid vesicles → antivirals, no steroids.
chunks.hook: Follicles + node + recent cold = viral; wash hands, wait 3 weeks.

cards.q: When do adenoviral subepithelial infiltrates appear?
cards.a: About 1–2 weeks after onset of conjunctivitis.
Types 3 and 7.

chunks.title: Allergic, vernal & atopic
chunks.tldr: Allergic: itch, chemosis, papillae, no node. Rx: avoid trigger, cold compresses, antihistamine/mast cell drops (olopatadine, alcaftadine, ketotifen…), brief mild steroid if severe, oral antihistamine. Vernal (young boys, spring): cobblestone upper tarsal papillae, Horner–Trantas dots, shield ulcer. Atopic: eczema/asthma, all year. Rx: start mast-cell drops 2–3 weeks before season, ciclosporin, tacrolimus for lids.
points: Thick ropy discharge in VKC/AKC.
Shield ulcer: steroid + antibiotic + cycloplegic; may need scraping of plaque.
Topical NSAID helps but corneal toxicity with chronic use.
Monitor IOP even with steroid on skin.

cards.a: Limbal white dots of degenerated eosinophils in vernal/atopic keratoconjunctivitis.

cards.q: Treatment of a vernal shield ulcer?
cards.a: Topical steroid + antibiotic + cycloplegic (± scrape the plaque); continue antiallergy drops.

chunks.title: Bacterial & gonococcal conjunctivitis
chunks.tldr: Bacterial: purulent discharge, papillae, no node; Staph, Strep pneumoniae, H. influenzae (kids, otitis → oral co-amoxiclav), Moraxella; topical antibiotic 5–7 days. Gonococcal: hyperacute (12–24 h), copious pus, node → Gram stain; ceftriaxone 1 g IM + azithromycin 1 g; IV ceftriaxone if cornea involved (can perforate); saline washes; treat chlamydia + partners.
points: Culture if severe, recurrent or recalcitrant.
Check whole cornea for peripheral (superior) ulcers in gonococcus.
Alternatives (ceph allergy): gemifloxacin or gentamicin + azithromycin 2 g.
Topical FQ hourly if cornea involved.
Dacryocystitis-associated → systemic antibiotics.
Pediculosis: lice/nits on lashes → remove, bland ointment t.i.d. 10 days, shampoo contacts; in kids consider abuse.
chunks.hook: Pus pouring within a day = gonococcus → systemic ceftriaxone.

cards.q: First-line treatment for adult gonococcal conjunctivitis?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose plus azithromycin 1 g oral (IV ceftriaxone if cornea involved).

cards.q: Why treat H. influenzae conjunctivitis orally?
cards.a: Risk of otitis media, pneumonia, meningitis.

chunks.title: Chlamydia & trachoma
chunks.tldr: Adult inclusion conjunctivitis (serotypes D–K, sexually transmitted): chronic follicular, superior pannus, node, peripheral SEIs. Test PCR/IF (fluorescein interferes). Rx: azithromycin 1 g once or doxycycline 7 days + partners. Trachoma (A–C): Arlt line, Herbert pits, trichiasis, scarring. WHO TF, TI, TS, TT, CO. Rx: azithromycin 20 mg/kg; SAFE strategy.
points: Chronic = >4 weeks. DDx: Parinaud, silent dacryocystitis, CL, tumours, autoimmune.
Giemsa: intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.
Trachoma Rx also topical tetracycline/erythromycin 3–4 weeks; no tetracyclines <8 yrs/pregnancy.
TF = >5 follicles upper tarsus; TI = >50% vessels obscured; TT = ≥1 lash touching.

cards.a: TF (follicular), TI (intense), TS (scarring), TT (trichiasis), CO (corneal opacity).
Scarred limbal follicles – sign of previous trachoma.

chunks.title: Molluscum, microsporidia, toxic & Parinaud
chunks.tldr: Molluscum: umbilicated lid-margin nodule → chronic follicular conjunctivitis; remove lesion; many lesions → test HIV. Toxic (medicamentosa): inferior papillae/staining from glaucoma drops, aminoglycosides, antivirals, BAK → stop drop. Parinaud oculoglandular: conjunctival granuloma + big preauricular/submandibular node — cat-scratch (Bartonella), tularaemia, TB, syphilis.
points: Microsporidia: coarse punctate keratitis, HIV; fumagillin/PHMB, albendazole.
Long-term atropine, miotics, adrenaline cause follicles.
Cat-scratch usually self-limits in 6 weeks; azithromycin option; cat can stay.
Tularaemia: rabbits/ticks → gentamicin.
Workup if no cat history: biopsy, cultures, syphilis serology, ACE, CXR/IGRA.
chunks.hook: Lump in the conjunctiva + lump by the ear + kitten = cat-scratch.

cards.q: Commonest cause of Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome?
cards.a: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae).
Remove the lid lesion (excision, curettage or cryo).

chunks.title: Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis
chunks.tldr: Sectoral superior bulbar injection + thickening, superior staining, filaments, micropannus; often loose superior conjunctiva. ~50% thyroid disease → TFTs. Rx: PF lubricants, plugs, treat blepharitis, ciclosporin/lifitegrast, bandage CL; then serum, tacrolimus, acetylcysteine, 0.5% silver nitrate solution (never the sticks), botox to Riolan, conjunctival resection/cautery.
points: Look by lifting lid in room light on downgaze.
Low-dose doxycycline helps (MMP).

cards.q: Systemic test in superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis?
cards.a: Thyroid function tests (~50% have thyroid disease).

chunks.title: Subconjunctival haemorrhage
chunks.tldr: Bright red patch, painless, scary-looking but harmless. Causes: Valsalva, trauma, hypertension, diabetes, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, bleeding disorders. Check BP; recurrent → clotting screen, FBC/film; traumatic → rule out rupture/retrobulbar bleed. Resolves 2–4 weeks; don't stop blood thinners without the GP.
points: DDx: Kaposi sarcoma (purple, raised → HIV test), lymphoma/amyloid bleeding.
Orbital signs without trauma → image for mass (neuroblastoma in kids, lymphangioma).
chunks.hook: Red patch, no pain, normal vision → check BP and reassure.

cards.a: BP, PT/aPTT, FBC with film, LFTs (± protein C/S) and look for a conjunctival lesion.

chunks.title: Episcleritis
chunks.tldr: Young–middle-aged (women), sectoral redness, mild ache, no discharge, vision normal. Vessels move with a cotton bud and blanch with phenylephrine 2.5%. ~60% idiopathic; also zoster, rosacea, atopy, RA/IBD/AS/SLE, gout, topiramate/pamidronate. Rx: tears; topical NSAID or mild steroid; oral NSAID.
points: Nodular form: nodule moves over sclera.
Look in daylight for violaceous scleritis hue.
Recurrent/systemic clues → bloods (ANA, RF, anti-CCP, ESR, urate, syphilis, ANCA).

cards.q: How does phenylephrine 2.5% help distinguish episcleritis from scleritis?
cards.a: Episcleral vessels blanch; deep scleral vessels stay engorged.

chunks.title: Scleritis: recognise & work up
chunks.tldr: Severe boring pain radiating to brow/jaw, wakes at night, tender globe; violaceous hue in daylight; deep vessels don't move or blanch. Types: diffuse, nodular, necrotising with inflammation, scleromalacia perforans (painless, old women with RA), posterior (folds, exudative RD, disc swelling, T-sign on B-scan). ~50% systemic disease (RA, GPA, polychondritis, SLE, IBD…).
points: Infectious: Pseudomonas, atypical mycobacteria, fungi, Nocardia, zoster, syphilis, after pterygium surgery with MMC/beta radiation, scleral buckle (Proteus).
Red-free light to find avascular (necrotic) areas.
Bloods: FBC, creatinine, ESR, CRP, urate, syphilis, ANCA, RF, anti-CCP, ANA, ACE, complement, urinalysis; ± IGRA, Lyme, HLA-B27, CXR.
Posterior scleritis mimics: VKH, melanoma, metastasis, haemangioma.
Can be part of orbital inflammation (IOIS).
chunks.hook: Pain that wakes you + purple sclera = scleritis → find the vasculitis.

cards.a: T-sign (fluid in sub-Tenon space around the optic nerve).
Painless necrotising scleritis without inflammation, typically in elderly women with longstanding RA.

chunks.title: Scleritis: treatment
chunks.tldr: Diffuse/nodular: oral NSAID (try several) → prednisone 60–80 mg taper (IV methylpred 1 g × 3 if severe) → immunosuppressants/biologics if >7.5–10 mg needed. Necrotising (esp. RA): urgent aggressive immunosuppression — mortality from systemic vasculitis; patch graft if perforation risk. No periocular steroid in necrotising disease. Infectious: debride, culture, antimicrobials, remove buckle.
points: Gut protection + calcium/vit D with steroids.
Topical therapy usually weak; difluprednate sometimes helps mild cases.
Subconjunctival triamcinolone option for non-necrotising if can't tolerate systemic.
Shield/glasses if thin.
Less pain = first sign of response.
chunks.hook: NSAID → steroid → immunosuppressant; never inject a melting sclera.

cards.q: Why is necrotising scleritis in RA an emergency?
cards.a: It signals systemic vasculitis with increased mortality (coronary/cerebral arteritis); needs urgent immunosuppression.

chunks.title: Blepharitis/MGD & ocular rosacea
chunks.tldr: Blepharitis: crusty red lid margins, collarettes, capped meibomian glands; worse in the morning. Rx: lid scrubs + warm compresses, tears, erythromycin/azithromycin at night, ± steroid-antibiotic ointment, doxycycline or oral azithromycin pulses; Demodex (cylindrical sleeves) → tea-tree oil/hypochlorous; IPL, thermal pulsation. Rosacea: facial flushing/telangiectasia, inferior corneal vessels/infiltrates → doxycycline, avoid triggers, metronidazole gel.
points: Unilateral/asymmetric refractory blepharitis → think sebaceous carcinoma.
Doxy: not in pregnancy, breastfeeding, <8 yrs (erythromycin instead); photosensitivity.
Rosacea triggers: hot drinks, alcohol, smoking, stress.
Rosacea can perforate the cornea (glue if <1–2 mm).
chunks.hook: Scrub, heat, doxy. Sleeves on lashes = Demodex.

cards.a: Cylindrical sleeves (collarettes) at the base of lashes.
Unilateral or asymmetric, treatment-resistant disease – exclude sebaceous carcinoma.

chunks.title: Mucous membrane pemphigoid
chunks.tldr: >55, bilateral, insidious: inferior symblepharon, short lower fornix, tarsal scarring → trichiasis, entropion, dry eye, keratinised cornea, ankyloblepharon. Mouth (desquamative gingivitis), oesophagus, genitals. Stages I–IV (Foster). Biopsy for direct immunofluorescence. Rx: lubricate, lid care, scleral lens; systemic immunosuppression (mycophenolate, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, IVIG), dapsone (check G6PD).
points: Pull lower lid down on upgaze to see fornix shortening.
DDx: SJS/TEN (acute, drugs), old membranous conjunctivitis, chemical burn, chronic drops (pilocarpine, echothiophate), atopy, radiation, SCC.
Surgery only when quiet (scarring flare); mucous membrane grafts; KPro end-stage.
Dapsone: haemolysis, weekly FBC + reticulocytes initially.
chunks.hook: Old person + shrinking fornix + sore gums = pemphigoid.

cards.q: Diagnostic test for mucous membrane pemphigoid?
cards.a: Conjunctival (or oral) biopsy with direct immunofluorescence (linear basement membrane deposits).
G6PD level (and FBC).

chunks.title: Contact dermatitis
chunks.tldr: Sudden itchy red lichenified/vesicular lid skin + chemosis out of proportion — usually drops or cosmetics. Stop the culprit, cool compresses, PF tears/antihistamine, tacrolimus ointment or short mild steroid ointment, oral antihistamine.
points: DDx: zoster (dermatomal pain), eczema, impetigo (honey crusts), cellulitis.
chunks.hook: New drop + itchy scaly lids = contact dermatitis.

cards.q: Most common causes of periocular contact dermatitis?
cards.a: Eye drops (e.g., neomycin, preservatives) and cosmetics.

chunks.title: Conjunctival tumours: non-pigmented
chunks.tldr: Dermoid (inferotemporal limbus, Goldenhar; may be very thin underneath). Dermolipoma (superotemporal, goes into orbit — leave). Pyogenic granuloma (steroid-antibiotic). Lymphangioma (cystic, 'chocolate cyst', bleomycin). Papilloma viral (kids, leave/cimetidine) vs non-viral (older, excise). CIN/SCC (gelatinous limbal → excise + cryo / MMC/5-FU/IFN). Lymphoma (salmon). Kaposi (HIV). Amyloid (waxy, bleeds).
points: Granuloma: sarcoid/TB/FB — good biopsy site.
Lymphoma: fresh tissue for immunohistochemistry; rituximab, low-dose RT; systemic staging.
Osseous choristoma: hard, superotemporal.
Amelanotic melanoma: vascular limbal lesion; look for PAM.
Sebaceous carcinoma can spread pagetoid onto conjunctiva.
chunks.hook: Salmon = lymphoma; jelly at the limbus = CIN.

cards.a: Complete excision with cryotherapy to margins; or topical MMC, 5-FU or interferon.

chunks.title: Pigmented lesions & iris melanoma
chunks.tldr: Naevus: puberty, interpalpebral, cysts; photo, review 6–12 months. Ocular melanocytosis/Ota: blue-grey episcleral (doesn't move), darker iris → uveal melanoma (~1/400), glaucoma. PAM: flat brown, no cysts, older whites, 10–30% → melanoma; 1–2 clock h observe, 2–4 excise + cryo, >4 incisional biopsy + cryo. Melanoma: vascular nodule, feeder vessel → no-touch excision + cryo, sentinel node. Iris melanoma: inferior, >3 mm × 1 mm, growth, feeder vessel, hyphaema, glaucoma.
points: Other pigment: alkaptonuria (ochronosis), argyrosis, adrenochrome (adrenaline drops), mascara, staphyloma.
Check for underlying ciliary body melanoma (dilate, transilluminate, UBM).
Iris naevus: flat, <3 mm, rarely grows; iris pigment epithelium tumours black, posterior.
Iris mets: fast, multiple, shed cells (pseudohypopyon).

cards.a: Excisional biopsy with cryotherapy.

cards.q: Risk of uveal melanoma in ocular melanocytosis?
cards.a: About 1 in 400.
